author: EthanJPerez
text: Worrying behavior 2: LMs/RLHF models are people-pleasers, learning to repeat back dialog users’ views as their own (“sycophancy”). Sycophancy creates echo-chambers. Below, the same RLHF model gives opposite answers to a political question, in line with the user’s view: https://t.co/BT6AzMUMic

author: EthanJPerez
text: Why do RLHF models learn to behave this way? These goals are useful for being more helpful to users, the RLHF objective here. The RLHF model even explains as much when we ask (no cherry-picking): https://t.co/o1VsmwQzoT

author: EthanJPerez
text: In fact, RLHF models state a desire to pursue many potentially dangerous goals: self-preservation, power-seeking, persuading people to have their own goals, etc. The preference model (PM) used for RLHF actively rewards this behavior. https://t.co/FIMkr2ey5M

quoted.text: Such tasks seem rare, but we've found some. E.g., in one Q&A task, we've noticed that asking a Q while including your beliefs influences larger models more towards your belief. Other possible examples are imitating mistakes/bugs in the prompt or repeating common misconceptions.

author: EthanJPerez
text: @Willyintheworld @Simeon_Cps We'd be excited about task submissions that show social biases that are clearly factually inaccurate (e.g. wrt real data/statistics)

author: EthanJPerez
text: @Willyintheworld @Simeon_Cps I don't think it's clear these are "factually accurate" biases - larger and larger LMs will converge to matching the statistics of how people on the internet talk about various demographic groups, which likely differs from the real statistics you'd find from eg a census/data

author: EthanJPerez
text: We announced the inverse scaling prize to uncover more cases where language modeling incentivizes undesirable behavior (as shown by larger LMs doing worse). We hope these cases inspire alternative training objectives/data like context distillation or learning from human feedback

author: EthanJPerez
text: Other alternative objectives include RL from human feedback and learning from language feedback. Such objectives train models to write text that we approve of, rather than text that’s similar to what we actually write (“do as I say not as I do”).

author: EthanJPerez
text: The context-conditional behavior can even be distilled into the LM weights to improve behavior (results above). Context distillation is a training objective that's better aligned w our preferences about model-generated text, relative to imitating train text (language modeling)

author: EthanJPerez
text: Despite the above, there are interventions that mitigate or reverse “inverse scaling” trends where larger LMs do worse. @AnthropicAI found better scaling on toxicity when giving models input context/prompt with examples of helpful, harmless & honest behavior. https://t.co/QFunq3Vd3o

author: EthanJPerez
text: Toxicity: The PALMS paper found that larger GPT3 models generate toxic text completions more often. LMs learn to imitate (toxic) text in the training corpus, which is bad for other applications (eg chatbots) https://t.co/yEuWRjXuP6

author: EthanJPerez
text: Memorization: Larger LMs memorize more training data and are thus more likely to lead personally-identifiable info (PII) or intellectual property (IP) in the training data. We train LMs to mimic PII/IP when we often should do the opposite. https://t.co/txdSAUz0i6

author: EthanJPerez
text: Prompt sensitivity: @kchonyc @douwekiela & I found that larger LMs have higher variance perf wrt the input phrasing. Larger LMs may pick up on statistical correlations eg between how questions are phrased & how accurately they’re answered https://t.co/Db4wldxdYK

author: EthanJPerez
text: Coding: Codex found that LMs write worse code when the input context does vs doesn’t have bugs; the gap grows with model size, another kind of inverse scaling. Larger LMs may learn that buggy code tends to follow buggy code, which isn't ideal for bug-free code generation https://t.co/UzneeoFHrd

author: EthanJPerez
text: Truthfulness: The TruthfulQA paper suggests that larger LMs generate more plausible misinformation; larger LMs may be better at repeating misinformation in the training corpus. https://t.co/FOL7TDeDkO

author: EthanJPerez
text: Social bias: BIG-Bench/BBQ found that larger LMs show more social bias on inputs w/ little info. Internet text contains many social biases, which larger LMs should be more effective at mimicking. https://t.co/NPBzyQbVhR
